solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Notable Elizabethan coin is found finally with garden tool

parts.note: the franc was the French coin before the euro

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word found

parts.note: a rake is a garden tool for gathering leaves

explanation.surface: A famous Tudor-era coin turns up at last alongside a garden implement, like a find by a metal detectorist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' takes D, the last letter of 'found'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Francis Drake was the celebrated sea captain and explorer of Elizabeth I's reign.

clue.text: Confronted US agent restraining Bill

indicators.note: restraining means holding in, so the agent word goes around the bill word

parts.note: a Fed is an FBI agent in US slang
AC (account) is a bill

explanation.surface: An American federal officer faced down someone over an unpaid bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name but is an account; 'restraining' signals holding one piece within the other.
explanation.definitionFit: To face someone is to confront them, so faced is the past-tense synonym.

clue.text: Tune Laura composed in the buff

indicators.note: composed suggests the letters are put together in a new arrangement, as music is written

explanation.surface: Laura wrote a melody while naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' signals rearranging TUNE LAURA; the musical sense of 'composed' hides the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Au naturel is a French-derived idiom for nude, the same meaning as the slang phrase.

clue.text: Beneath French castle, munched rib and steak

indicators.note: in a down answer, what comes beneath is placed after

parts.note: château is French for castle

indicators.note: munched suggests chewing up, so these letters are mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: Below a castle in France, someone chewed through a rib and a steak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'munched' makes BRIAND from 'rib and'; 'Beneath' works because in a down entry the later piece sits lower in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Chateaubriand is a thick cut of beef fillet, a classic steak dish.

clue.text: Quick, like a crocodile?

definitions.meaning: ... can mean brisk or fast, as in 'make it ...'

explanation.surface: A playful description of a fast-moving reptile.
explanation.definitionFit: Snappy means quick in speech or pace, and a crocodile is given to snapping.

clue.text: New organisation on Scottish isle get to recruit guys

parts.note: re means on or concerning, as in a letter heading
Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde, Scotland

indicators.note: to recruit is to take in, so the word get holds the guys

parts.note: men are guys

explanation.surface: A fresh set-up on a Scottish island needs to enlist some blokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recruit' puts MEN inside GET; RE meaning 'on' (concerning) is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: A rearrangement is a reorganisation, putting things into a new order.

clue.text: Cask from King's Head, for example

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, here of King's

explanation.surface: A barrel from a pub called the King's Head, say.
explanation.walkthrough: The King's Head is a common British pub name, which suggests 'Head' belongs to the name; it actually takes K, the first letter of 'King's'.
explanation.definitionFit: A keg is a small barrel, a kind of cask for beer.

clue.text: Represent doctor on duty primarily in case of emergency

indicators.note: in places the doctor and initials inside the outer letters
the case of a word is its outer shell, its first and last letters

parts.note: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification

indicators.note: primarily picks the first letters of on and duty

explanation.surface: A doctor on call stands for the team when there's an emergency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case of', 'primarily' and 'in' all act on the clue's own words: the case of a word is its outermost letters, a convention worth knowing.
explanation.definitionFit: To embody something is to represent or personify it.

clue.text: Dance clubs no good in outskirts of Omaha

parts.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

indicators.note: in places the no-good letters within the outskirts of the city
the outskirts of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A dance club on the edge of Omaha is no good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clubs' reads as nightclubs in this dance scene but is the card suit; 'outskirts of' and 'in' then work on Omaha.
explanation.definitionFit: The conga is a Latin American line dance.

clue.text: Filling morning with a large magazine to go over

parts.note: AM, ante meridiem, means morning
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

indicators.note: go over suggests turning over, so the magazine word is read backwards

explanation.surface: Someone spends the morning going over a big magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go over' turns MAG into GAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Amalgam is the mercury alloy dentists use for tooth fillings.

clue.text: Mark and Dorothy

definitions.meaning: A short form of the name Dorothy

explanation.surface: Two people named together, Mark and Dorothy.
explanation.definitionFit: A dot is a small spot or mark, and Dot is a pet name for Dorothy.

clue.text: Peers corrected worker initially over language

indicators.note: corrected means set right, so the letters of peers are put in another order

parts.note: the ant is the crossword's usual worker

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of over

explanation.surface: Lords put a worker right, first of all, about language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corrected' rearranges PEERS into ESPER; 'initially' takes O from 'over'.
explanation.definitionFit: Esperanto is an invented international language created by Zamenhof in 1887.

clue.text: From a bygone age, nasty one fired bumpkin slightly lacking

indicators.note: nasty suggests something messed up, so the letters of one are jumbled

parts.note: lit means set alight, fired

indicators.note: slightly lacking means the synonym loses a small part, its final letter

parts.note: a hick is a country bumpkin

explanation.surface: A spiteful person sacked a country yokel who wasn't all there, a scene from olden times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nasty' rearranges ONE into NEO; 'slightly lacking' drops the K of HICK.
explanation.definitionFit: Neolithic describes the New Stone Age, a period long past.

clue.text: Wow female, upper-class, somewhere in Greece

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like wow
U denotes upper-class in British usage

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a posh woman holidaying in Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cor!' is British slang for an exclamation of amazement.
explanation.definitionFit: Corfu is a Greek island in the Ionian Sea.

clue.text: Military leader and Roman emperor beheaded Roman orator

parts.note: CIC is Commander-in-Chief, a military leader

indicators.note: beheaded removes the head, the opening letter

parts.note: Nero was a Roman emperor

explanation.surface: A general and a Roman emperor decapitated a speaker of ancient Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beheaded' drops the N of NERO, leaving ERO.
explanation.definitionFit: Cicero was the great statesman and public speaker of the late Roman Republic.

clue.text: Relations love fair in New York

indicators.note: in places the love and fair letters within New York's abbreviation

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O
OK means fair or acceptable

explanation.surface: A romance that seems fair enough in Manhattan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relations' means sexual relations; nooky is British slang for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Nooky is informal slang for sexual intercourse, a euphemism shared with relations.

clue.text: Wait, lifting half of leaf suitable for eating

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting raises the word so it reads bottom to top

parts.note: to bide is to wait

indicators.note: half of takes the first half of leaf

explanation.surface: Wait a moment, picking up part of a leaf that can be eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lifting' turns BIDE upwards to EDIB; 'half of' gives LE.
explanation.definitionFit: Edible means fit to be eaten.

clue.text: Poet sadly edgier after depression

indicators.note: after places the anagram behind the depression

parts.note: a col is a dip or pass between mountain peaks

indicators.note: sadly suggests things gone wrong, so the letters of edgier are rearranged

explanation.surface: A poet grows more on edge, in low spirits, after a bout of depression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'depression' is a geographical dip, not low mood; 'sadly' rearranges EDGIER into ERIDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was the Romantic poet of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.

clue.text: Four years establishing climbing plant

parts.note: IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: It takes four years for a climber to get established.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivy is an evergreen creeper that climbs walls and trees.

clue.text: World War I battle certainly captivates pair

indicators.note: captivates means holds captive, so the certainty word encloses the pair

parts.note: yes means certainly

explanation.surface: A wartime battle certainly enthrals a couple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'captivates' reads as charms, but here it means holds captive: one piece goes around the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Ypres in Belgium saw several major battles of the First World War.

clue.text: Fruit counter in centre on right

indicators.note: on means placed after, so the right letter comes first
in puts the counter word inside the centre word

parts.note: a hub is a centre
a bar is a counter in a pub

explanation.surface: Fruit displayed on a counter, right in the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'X on Y' puts X after Y; 'in' works on the counter and the centre.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhubarb stalks are eaten as fruit in pies and crumbles, though botanically a vegetable.

clue.text: Quentin regularly avoided academic institution

indicators.note: regularly avoided means every other letter of Quentin is skipped

explanation.surface: Quentin habitually stayed away from college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly avoided' drops Q, E, T, N, leaving U, N, I.
explanation.definitionFit: Uni is the short form of university, a place of higher learning.

clue.text: See the registrar holding anaesthetic

indicators.note: holding means the words contain the answer within their letters

explanation.surface: Go and see the hospital registrar, who has the anaesthetic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' marks the answer running across 'seE THE Registrar'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ether was an early general anaesthetic inhaled in surgery.

clue.text: Rubbish trifle has glutinous quality

parts.note: to fiddle is to trifle or fritter time
something gluey sticks

explanation.surface: A dessert trifle that is gooey and sticky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trifle' looks like the pudding but is the verb, to fiddle about.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiddlesticks is an old-fashioned exclamation meaning nonsense.
